title: Fractions — Parts of a Whole
blurb: What a fraction really is — equal parts of a whole — unit and non-unit fractions, comparing them, and taking a fraction of a set, drawn with fraction bars throughout.

lessons.title: Equal Parts
lessons.concreteComparison: Two friends share one khuushuur. Cut it in the middle and each holds one half — a fair share with a name. Cut it crooked, one big piece and one small, and NOBODY holds a half: just a lucky friend and an unlucky one. A fraction is born only when the parts are EQUAL.
lessons.objective: Decide whether a cut makes equal parts, name equal parts from their count — halves, thirds, quarters — and read the bottom number of a fraction as the number of equal parts.
concept: **A fraction needs equal parts.** Cut a whole into parts of the SAME size and each part earns a fraction name. Parts of different sizes have no fraction name at all — a big piece and a small piece are just pieces.
**The count names the parts.** $2$ equal parts are HALVES, $3$ are THIRDS, $4$ are QUARTERS, $5$ are fifths. The name comes straight from how many equal parts make the whole.

**The bottom number cuts.** Written as a fraction, the bottom number says how many equal parts the whole is cut into: in $\frac{1}{4}$ the $4$ means four equal parts, and the $1$ on top counts one of them.
lessons.keyIdea: Equal parts, or no fraction at all. The bottom number cuts the whole into that many equal parts; the top number counts the parts you take.

facts.title: The naming rule
facts.explanation: Count the equal parts; the count is the name.

facts.title: The parts rebuild the whole
facts.explanation: Four quarter-pieces put back together make exactly one whole — the test of a fair cut.

workedExamples.statement: A khuushuur is cut into $2$ equal parts. What is each part called, and how many of them rebuild the whole?
workedExamples.note: Equal parts first — then the count gives the name.
workedExamples.solution: Two EQUAL parts: each is one half, written $\frac{1}{2}$. Two halves rebuild the whole: $2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1$ ✓.

workedExamples.statement: Saraa cuts a ribbon into $4$ parts, but two are long and two are short. May any part be called one quarter?
workedExamples.note: Count the parts AND check their sizes.
workedExamples.solution: No. A quarter means one of $4$ EQUAL parts — four true quarters rebuild the whole exactly, $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$. Saraa's parts differ in size, so none of them earns the name.

commonMistakes.text: Calling one of 4 unequal pieces "a quarter" just because there are 4 pieces.
commonMistakes.correction: A quarter is one of 4 EQUAL pieces. Count the pieces and check their sizes — if the sizes differ, the name does not apply.

commonMistakes.text: Reading the bottom number as "how many pieces I take".
commonMistakes.correction: The bottom number CUTS: it says how many equal parts make the whole. The top number is the one that counts what you take.

tryIt.statement: A round bread is cut into $3$ equal parts. Name one part in words and as a fraction.
tryIt.solution: Three equal parts are thirds: one part is one third, $\frac{1}{3}$. Three of them rebuild the bread: $3 \times \frac{1}{3} = 1$ ✓.

tryIt.statement: In the fraction $\frac{1}{5}$, what does the $5$ tell you, and what does the $1$ tell you?
tryIt.solution: The $5$ cuts: the whole is in $5$ equal parts. The $1$ counts: you take one part. Five such parts make the whole: $5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1$ ✓.

steps.title: Equal parts, or no fraction
beats: Two friends share one khuushuur. Cut it in the middle: $2$ EQUAL parts, and each friend holds one half — the bar below shows the fair cut.
Cut it crooked instead — one big part, one small — and neither part is a half. It is just a big piece and a small piece, with no fraction name.
That is the first rule of fractions: a fraction names one of EQUAL parts. No equal parts, no fraction.

steps.title: Fair cut or not?
steps.intro: Check the sizes before giving any part a name.

examples.prompt: A khuushuur is cut into $2$ equal parts. What is each part?
steps: Equal sizes, $2$ parts: each is one half.
Two halves rebuild the whole: $2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1$ ✓.

examples.prompt: Saraa cuts a ribbon into $4$ parts: two long, two short. Is any part one quarter?
steps: Four parts, but NOT equal — sizes differ.
No part is a quarter: quarters are $4$ equal parts, and $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ only works for a fair cut.

steps.title: Spot the fair cut
steps.intro: Equal sizes first, names second.

problems.prompt: A pizza is cut into $2$ equal slices. Each slice is:
problems.explanation: Two EQUAL parts are halves, and two halves rebuild the pizza: $2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1$ ✓. A quarter would need $4$ equal parts, and a whole is the uncut pizza itself.

problems.prompt: A chocolate bar snaps into $3$ pieces: one big, two tiny. Is each piece one third?
options: no — thirds must be three EQUAL pieces
yes — three pieces always make thirds
only the big piece is one third
problems.explanation: Check sizes before names: thirds are three EQUAL pieces, and three of them rebuild the bar, $3 \times \frac{1}{3} = 1$ ✓. Counting three pieces without checking sizes is the trap.

problems.prompt: How many EQUAL parts does a whole cut into quarters have?
problems.explanation: Quarters means four equal parts — $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ✓. Two equal parts would be halves, three would be thirds.

steps.title: The equal-parts rule
steps.prompt: A cake is cut into $4$ parts of DIFFERENT sizes, and one part is on your plate. Do you hold one quarter of the cake?
options: no — a quarter needs $4$ EQUAL parts
yes — one part of four is always a quarter
yes, if your part is the biggest
yes, if your part is the smallest
steps.explanation: The name quarter belongs to a fair cut only: four EQUAL parts, each $\frac{1}{4}$, rebuilding the cake as $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ✓. One unequal part of four could be almost any amount, so the name would lie.

steps.title: Folding is a fair cutter
steps.body: Fold a strip of paper in half and the crease cuts it into $2$ equal parts. Fold it in half again: $2 \times 2 = 4$ equal parts — quarters. One more fold gives $2 \times 4 = 8$ equal parts. Every fold doubles the count of equal parts, and a fold never cheats — the two sides land exactly on each other.

steps.title: The count is the name
beats: Equal parts are named by their COUNT: $2$ equal parts are halves, $3$ are thirds, $4$ are quarters, $5$ are fifths, $6$ are sixths — the bar below shows quarters.
Write it with two numbers: the BOTTOM number says how many equal parts the whole is cut into; the TOP number counts how many parts you take. One part of four is $\frac{1}{4}$.
Say the rule the way you will use it all topic: THE BOTTOM NUMBER CUTS, THE TOP NUMBER COUNTS.

steps.title: Name the parts
steps.intro: Count the equal parts; the count is the name.

examples.prompt: A bread is cut into $3$ equal parts and you take one. Write the fraction.
steps: Three equal parts: thirds. One of them is one third.
Bottom cuts ($3$ equal parts), top counts ($1$ taken): $\frac{1}{3}$.

examples.prompt: What are $8$ equal parts of a whole called, and what fraction is one part?
steps: Eight equal parts: eighths.
One part is $\frac{1}{8}$, and eight of them rebuild the whole: $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ ✓.

steps.title: Bottom cuts, top counts
steps.intro: Read both numbers, in that order.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $6$ equal parts with $1$ shaded. The shaded part is:
problems.explanation: Bottom cuts: $6$ equal parts. Top counts: $1$ shaded. So $\frac{1}{6}$, and $6 \times \frac{1}{6} = 1$ rebuilds the bar ✓. $\frac{6}{1}$ swaps the two jobs, and $\frac{1}{5}$ miscounts the parts.

problems.prompt: $5$ equal parts of a whole are called:
problems.explanation: The count names the parts: five equal parts are fifths, each $\frac{1}{5}$, and $5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1$ ✓. Halves would mean only two equal parts.

problems.prompt: In $\frac{1}{4}$, the $4$ tells you:
options: the whole is cut into $4$ equal parts
problems.explanation: The bottom number cuts: $4$ equal parts make the whole, so each is $\frac{1}{4}$ and $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ✓. Taking parts is the top number's job.

steps.title: Read the bottom number
steps.prompt: A bar is cut into $9$ equal pieces. One piece is:
steps.explanation: Bottom cuts: $9$ equal pieces, so one piece is $\frac{1}{9}$, and nine of them rebuild the bar: $9 \times \frac{1}{9} = 1$ ✓. Writing $\frac{9}{1}$ swaps cutter and counter.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A fraction names one of EQUAL parts — unequal pieces have no fraction name.
The count names the parts: 2 halves, 3 thirds, 4 quarters, 5 fifths.
The bottom number cuts the whole into equal parts.
The top number counts the parts you take.
All the parts together rebuild exactly one whole.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every picture below, ask two questions in order: are the parts EQUAL, and how many are there? Only then give the name.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Fair cuts, names, and the two numbers.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $5$ equal parts with $1$ shaded. The shaded part is:
problems.explanation: Five equal parts, one taken: $\frac{1}{5}$, and $5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{1}{4}$ miscounts the cut; $\frac{5}{1}$ puts the cutter on top.

problems.prompt: Temuulen cuts a melon into $2$ pieces, one clearly bigger than the other. The smaller piece is:
options: not a half — the parts are not equal
one half of the bigger piece
problems.explanation: Halves demand two EQUAL parts, so that $2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1$ ✓. An uneven cut makes pieces without fraction names — counting two pieces is not enough.

problems.prompt: Which cut turns a bread into quarters?
problems.explanation: Quarters are $4$ EQUAL parts — each $\frac{1}{4}$, together $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ✓. Any-size parts break the equal rule, and $2$ equal parts are halves.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $8$ equal parts with $1$ shaded. Shaded part and its name:
problems.explanation: Count the cut: $8$ equal parts, so one is $\frac{1}{8}$ and $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ ✓. One sixth belongs to a $6$-part cut.

problems.prompt: The bottom number of a fraction always tells you:
options: how many equal parts the whole is cut into
problems.explanation: The bottom cuts, the top counts. A bottom of $7$ means seven equal parts, each $\frac{1}{7}$, and $7 \times \frac{1}{7} = 1$ ✓. What you take is the top number's story.

steps.title: You've finished "Equal Parts"
steps.body: Equal parts, and names straight from the count — the ground every fraction stands on. Next: the fractions made of exactly ONE part, from $\frac{1}{2}$ all the way down to $\frac{1}{10}$, and a surprise about which of them is biggest.

lessons.title: Unit Fractions
lessons.concreteComparison: One slab of aaruul, and hungry cousins keep arriving. Shared by $2$, each gets a big half. Shared by $4$, each gets a smaller quarter. Shared by $10$, each gets a thin tenth. The slab never grew or shrank — but the MORE people share it, the SMALLER each share becomes.
lessons.objective: Read and write the unit fractions $\frac{1}{2}$ to $\frac{1}{10}$, know how many of each rebuild the whole, and use the rule that more parts make each part smaller.
concept: **A unit fraction is ONE part.** Cut a whole into equal parts and take exactly one: $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{1}{4}$, down to $\frac{1}{10}$. The top is always $1$; only the cut changes.
**The bottom number promises a rebuild.** Cut into $8$, and $8$ pieces of $\frac{1}{8}$ make the whole again: $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$. Whatever the cut, all its pieces together are exactly $1$.

**More parts, smaller pieces.** The same whole shared into more parts leaves less for each: $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{4}$, even though $8 > 4$. For unit fractions the bigger bottom number means the smaller piece.
lessons.keyIdea: A unit fraction is one piece of an equal cut, and the finer the cut, the smaller the piece: the bigger the bottom number, the less you hold.

facts.title: One piece of the cut
facts.explanation: Top always 1 — one piece. The bottom says how fine the cut is.

facts.title: More parts, smaller pieces
facts.explanation: Eight pieces share the same whole that four shared — so each eighth is smaller.

workedExamples.statement: A bar is cut into $8$ equal pieces. Write the fraction for one piece, and say how many pieces rebuild the bar.
workedExamples.solution: One piece of an $8$-cut is $\frac{1}{8}$. Eight of them rebuild the bar: $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ ✓.

workedExamples.statement: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{4}$ of a bar, or $\frac{1}{8}$ of the same bar?
workedExamples.note: Same whole — compare how many pieces share it.
workedExamples.solution: $\frac{1}{4}$: only $4$ pieces share the whole, so each is big. $\frac{1}{8}$: $8$ pieces share the same whole, so each is smaller. $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{4}$, even though $8 > 4$.

commonMistakes.text: Thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4.
commonMistakes.correction: The bottom number counts how many pieces SHARE the whole: more sharers, smaller shares. So 1/8 < 1/4 — the bigger bottom loses.

commonMistakes.text: Writing one piece of a 5-cut as 5/1.
commonMistakes.correction: The bottom cuts, the top counts: one piece of 5 equal pieces is 1/5. Putting the 5 on top would claim five wholes.

tryIt.statement: Cut a bar into $10$ equal pieces. What fraction is one piece, and how many rebuild the whole?
tryIt.solution: One piece is $\frac{1}{10}$; ten of them rebuild the bar: $10 \times \frac{1}{10} = 1$ ✓.

steps.title: One piece of the cut
beats: A UNIT fraction is exactly one piece of an equal cut. The bar below is cut into $6$ equal pieces with $1$ shaded: that shaded piece is $\frac{1}{6}$.
The whole family looks alike: $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{5}$, all the way to $\frac{1}{10}$. The top is always $1$ — one piece — and the bottom says how fine the cut is.
Every cut keeps the rebuild promise: $6$ sixths make the whole, $10$ tenths make the whole. The bottom number cuts, and all its pieces together are exactly $1$.

steps.title: Write the unit fraction
steps.intro: Top 1, bottom the cut — then check the rebuild.

examples.prompt: A bar is cut into $8$ equal pieces. What fraction is one piece?
steps: Top $1$ (one piece), bottom $8$ (the cut): $\frac{1}{8}$.
Rebuild check: $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ ✓.

examples.prompt: How many $\frac{1}{7}$ pieces make one whole?
steps: The bottom promises the rebuild: a $7$-cut needs all $7$ pieces.

steps.title: The unit family
steps.intro: One piece each — read the cut.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $9$ equal pieces with $1$ shaded. The shaded piece is:
problems.explanation: Nine equal pieces, one taken: $\frac{1}{9}$, and $9 \times \frac{1}{9} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{9}{1}$ swaps cutter and counter; $\frac{1}{8}$ miscounts the cut.

problems.prompt: How many $\frac{1}{10}$ pieces rebuild one whole?
problems.explanation: The bottom's promise: a $10$-cut rebuilds from all $10$ pieces — $10 \times \frac{1}{10} = 1$ ✓. One piece alone is just $\frac{1}{10}$, far short of the whole.

problems.prompt: One slice of a pizza cut into $6$ equal slices is:
problems.explanation: Six equal slices, one taken: $\frac{1}{6}$, and $6 \times \frac{1}{6} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{6}{6}$ would be ALL the slices — the entire pizza.

steps.title: One piece, exactly
steps.prompt: Which fraction names ONE piece of a whole cut into $5$ equal pieces?
steps.explanation: Bottom cuts ($5$ equal pieces), top counts ($1$ piece): $\frac{1}{5}$, and $5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{5}{5}$ takes every piece — the whole — and $\frac{5}{1}$ swaps the numbers' jobs.

steps.title: Music runs on unit fractions
steps.body: Musicians name note lengths exactly like fractions: a half note lasts half as long as a whole note, a quarter note a quarter, an eighth note an eighth. Two half notes fill the time of one whole note, and it takes eight eighth notes to fill the same time — the more notes per whole, the shorter each one sounds.

steps.title: More parts, smaller pieces
beats: Take two same-size bars. Cut one into $4$ and the other into $8$. The bar below shows the $4$-cut: only $4$ pieces share the whole, so each piece is generous.
In the $8$-cut, twice as many pieces share the SAME whole — so every piece is smaller. $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{4}$, even though $8 > 4$.
The rule for every unit fraction: the bigger the bottom number, the finer the cut, the SMALLER the piece. The bottom cuts more, each piece gets less.

steps.title: Compare the cuts
steps.intro: Same whole — the finer cut makes the smaller piece.

examples.prompt: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{4}$ or $\frac{1}{8}$ of the same bar?
steps: The $4$-cut shares the whole among fewer pieces, so each is bigger.
$\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{4}$ — the bigger bottom loses.

fraction.label: eighths: 8 pieces share the same whole

examples.prompt: Order $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{1}{4}$ from biggest to smallest.
steps: Fewest sharers first: the $2$-cut gives the biggest piece.

steps.title: Bigger bottom, smaller piece
steps.intro: Picture the sharers before answering.

problems.prompt: Which is SMALLER: $\frac{1}{5}$ or $\frac{1}{9}$?
problems.explanation: Nine pieces share the whole that five shared: each ninth is smaller — $\frac{1}{9} < \frac{1}{5}$. Picking $\frac{1}{5}$ reads the bottoms forwards instead of backwards.

problems.prompt: Which piece is BIGGEST: $\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{1}{7}$, $\frac{1}{10}$?
problems.explanation: The coarsest cut wins: only $3$ pieces share the whole, so $\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{7} > \frac{1}{10}$. The $10$-cut has the most sharers and the thinnest pieces.

problems.prompt: Two same-size breads: one shared equally by $6$ people, one by $8$. A bigger share comes from:
problems.explanation: Fewer sharers, bigger shares: $\frac{1}{6} > \frac{1}{8}$. The $8$-person bread splits the same amount among more people.

steps.title: Backwards on purpose
options: $\frac{1}{10}$ is smaller — ten pieces share the whole
they are equal — both have $1$ on top
steps.explanation: Ten sharers against two: each tenth is a sliver, each half is generous — $\frac{1}{10} < \frac{1}{2}$. "Ten beats two" reads the bottom forwards; unit fractions read it backwards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A unit fraction is ONE piece of an equal cut: top always 1.
The bottom number says how fine the cut is — and promises the rebuild.
All the pieces of any cut together make exactly 1.
More parts means smaller pieces: 1/8 < 1/4.
For unit fractions, the bigger bottom number always loses.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before comparing two unit fractions, say out loud how many people share each whole — the crowd with more sharers gets the smaller piece.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Reading, rebuilding, and comparing unit fractions.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $7$ equal pieces with $1$ shaded. The shaded piece is:
problems.explanation: Seven equal pieces, one taken: $\frac{1}{7}$, and $7 \times \frac{1}{7} = 1$ ✓. The other options swap the numbers or miscount the cut.

problems.prompt: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{6}$ or $\frac{1}{4}$ of the same cake?
problems.explanation: Four sharers beat six: $\frac{1}{4} > \frac{1}{6}$. Choosing $\frac{1}{6}$ because $6 > 4$ is the forwards-reading trap.

problems.prompt: How many $\frac{1}{8}$ pieces rebuild one whole?
problems.explanation: The bottom's promise: $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ ✓. Four eighths reach only half the bar.

problems.prompt: One slab of aaruul is shared equally by $10$ children. Each child gets:
problems.explanation: Ten equal shares: each is $\frac{1}{10}$, and $10 \times \frac{1}{10} = 1$ rebuilds the slab ✓. $\frac{1}{9}$ would mean only nine sharers.

problems.prompt: Order from smallest to biggest: $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{8}$, $\frac{1}{4}$.
problems.explanation: Most sharers first: the $8$-cut gives the thinnest piece, the $2$-cut the fattest — $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{4} < \frac{1}{2}$. The second option reads the bottoms forwards.

steps.title: You've finished "Unit Fractions"
steps.body: One piece of every cut, and the backwards rule — bigger bottom, smaller piece. Next: taking MORE than one piece, where the top number finally starts counting past $1$.

lessons.title: Non-Unit Fractions
lessons.concreteComparison: A chocolate bar snaps into $4$ equal pieces. Each piece is $\frac{1}{4}$ — you know that. Now take THREE of them. You hold three pieces of the quarter size: $\frac{3}{4}$ of the bar. The top number finally earns its keep — it counts the pieces you took.
lessons.objective: Read and write non-unit fractions as several unit pieces, tell what the numerator and denominator each do, and recognise the fractions that equal one whole.
concept: **A non-unit fraction is a stack of unit pieces.** $\frac{3}{4}$ is three pieces of the $\frac{1}{4}$ size: $3 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$. Same cut as $\frac{1}{4}$ — just more pieces taken.

**The numerator counts, the denominator names.** Those are the proper names of the two numbers: the TOP number is the numerator, the BOTTOM number is the denominator. In $\frac{5}{8}$ the denominator $8$ names the cut (eighths) and the numerator $5$ counts the pieces taken. The bottom number cuts, the top number counts.

**When the top reaches the bottom, you hold the whole.** Take ALL $4$ quarters and you have $\frac{4}{4} = 1$ — the entire bar. Every cut has its whole-name: $\frac{6}{6}$, $\frac{8}{8}$, $\frac{10}{10}$ all equal $1$.
lessons.keyIdea: The top number counts pieces, the bottom number names the cut — and when the top reaches the bottom, the pieces rebuild exactly one whole.

facts.title: A stack of unit pieces
facts.explanation: Three quarter-pieces in one hand — that is all a non-unit fraction is.

facts.title: The whole, rebuilt
facts.explanation: All the pieces of the cut together: exactly one whole, never more, never less.

workedExamples.statement: A bar is cut into $4$ equal pieces and $3$ are shaded. What fraction is shaded, and what is it made of?
workedExamples.note: Name the cut first, then count the pieces.
workedExamples.solution: The cut: quarters, each $\frac{1}{4}$. The count: $3$ pieces. Shaded: $\frac{3}{4}$ — three pieces of the quarter size, $3 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.

workedExamples.statement: All $6$ pieces of a $6$-piece bar are shaded. Write the shaded fraction, and give its other name.
workedExamples.note: The top has reached the bottom.
workedExamples.solution: Shaded: $\frac{6}{6}$ — six pieces of the sixth size, $6 \times \frac{1}{6} = 1$. Its other name is $1$: the whole bar.

commonMistakes.text: Reading 3/4 as two separate numbers, "3 and 4".
commonMistakes.correction: A fraction is ONE amount: three pieces of the quarter size. The bar between the numbers is not a comma.
4/4 is four QUARTER pieces — together exactly one whole. The top counts pieces of the cut, not wholes.

tryIt.statement: A bar of $8$ equal pieces has $5$ shaded. What fraction is shaded, and what fraction is plain?
tryIt.solution: Shaded: $5$ pieces of the eighth size, $\frac{5}{8}$. Plain: the other $3$ pieces, $\frac{3}{8}$ — since $5 + 3 = 8$, together they use every piece of the bar.

tryIt.statement: Write the fraction with denominator $8$ that equals one whole.
tryIt.solution: $\frac{8}{8} = 1$: all eight eighth-pieces together rebuild the bar, $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ ✓.

steps.title: Stacks of unit pieces
beats: The bar below is cut into $4$ equal pieces and $3$ are shaded. Each piece is $\frac{1}{4}$; three of them together are $\frac{3}{4}$.
That is every non-unit fraction's secret: $\frac{3}{4}$ is just $3$ pieces of the $\frac{1}{4}$ size — $3 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.
The two numbers keep their jobs: THE BOTTOM NUMBER CUTS (quarters), THE TOP NUMBER COUNTS (three of them).
Both numbers have proper names too: the top number is the NUMERATOR (the counter) and the bottom number is the DENOMINATOR (the cutter). Same two jobs, longer names.

steps.title: Name the cut, count the pieces
steps.intro: Bottom first, top second — always that order.

examples.prompt: A bar of $8$ equal pieces has $5$ shaded. What fraction is shaded?
steps: The cut: eighths. The count: $5$ pieces.
$\frac{5}{8}$ — five pieces of the eighth size, $5 \times \frac{1}{8} = \frac{5}{8}$.

examples.prompt: You eat $2$ pieces of a khuushuur cut into $5$ equal pieces. What fraction did you eat?
steps: The cut: fifths. The count: $2$ eaten.
$\frac{2}{5}$ — two pieces of the fifth size, $2 \times \frac{1}{5} = \frac{2}{5}$.

steps.title: Top counts, bottom names
steps.intro: Read the picture in the rule's order.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $3$ equal pieces with $2$ shaded. The shaded fraction is:
problems.explanation: Cut into thirds, $2$ taken: $\frac{2}{3} = 2 \times \frac{1}{3}$ ✓. $\frac{3}{2}$ swaps the jobs, and $\frac{1}{3}$ counts only one piece.

problems.prompt: In $\frac{5}{6}$, the $5$ tells you:
options: the whole is cut into $5$ parts
problems.explanation: The top counts: five pieces of the sixth size, $5 \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$. Cutting is the bottom number's job — here the cut is $6$.

problems.prompt: $\frac{7}{10}$ means:
problems.explanation: Bottom cuts into tenths, top counts $7$ of them: $7 \times \frac{1}{10} = \frac{7}{10}$. Swapping the numbers' jobs is the trap in the second option.

steps.title: Count the shaded pieces
steps.prompt: A bar is cut into $8$ equal pieces and $3$ are shaded. The shaded fraction is:
steps.explanation: Cut: eighths. Count: $3$ shaded. So $\frac{3}{8} = 3 \times \frac{1}{8}$ ✓. $\frac{5}{8}$ counts the PLAIN pieces, $\frac{3}{5}$ compares shaded with plain instead of with the whole, and $\frac{8}{3}$ swaps the jobs.

steps.title: Quarter past, half past
steps.body: Clock talk is fraction talk. An hour is $60$ minutes, and a quarter of it is $60 \div 4 = 15$ minutes — so "quarter past three" means $15$ minutes after three o'clock. "Half past" uses $60 \div 2 = 30$. People tell fractions of an hour every single day without noticing.

steps.title: When the top reaches the bottom
beats: Take ALL the pieces of a cut and you hold the whole thing. The bar below has all $8$ of its $8$ pieces shaded: $\frac{8}{8} = 1$.
Every cut has a whole-name like this: $\frac{4}{4}$, $\frac{6}{6}$, $\frac{10}{10}$ — all of them exactly $1$, because all the pieces together rebuild the whole.
And the pieces always account for everything: if $5$ of $8$ pieces are shaded, the plain part is the other $3$ pieces — $\frac{3}{8}$. Shaded pieces and plain pieces use all $8$ between them.

steps.title: The whole, and the rest
steps.intro: All the pieces make 1; the plain part is the missing count.

examples.prompt: Write the fraction with denominator $10$ that equals one whole.
steps: All ten tenth-pieces: $\frac{10}{10}$.
Rebuild check: $10 \times \frac{1}{10} = 1$ ✓.

examples.prompt: A bar of $6$ equal pieces has $4$ shaded. What fraction is plain?
steps: Plain pieces: $6 - 4 = 2$, and $2 + 4 = 6$ ✓ accounts for every piece.
Plain fraction: $\frac{2}{6}$ — together with $\frac{4}{6}$ the bar is whole.

steps.title: Wholes and leftovers
steps.intro: The top meets the bottom, or falls short.

problems.prompt: Which fraction equals $1$?
problems.explanation: All nine ninth-pieces rebuild the whole: $9 \times \frac{1}{9} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{1}{9}$ is one thin piece, and $\frac{9}{10}$ stops one piece short of the whole.

problems.prompt: You walk $\frac{4}{10}$ of a path to the well. The fraction still ahead is:
problems.explanation: The path has $10$ tenth-parts; $4$ are behind you, so $10 - 4 = 6$ remain — $\frac{6}{10}$, and $6 + 4 = 10$ ✓ accounts for the whole path.

problems.prompt: How many $\frac{1}{6}$ pieces are inside $\frac{5}{6}$?
problems.explanation: $\frac{5}{6}$ is a stack of five sixth-pieces: $5 \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$ ✓. Six of them would already be the whole.

steps.title: The top meets the bottom
steps.explanation: Eight pieces of the eighth size: $8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1$ — the whole khuushuur, exactly. It is not $8$ khuushuur: the top counts pieces of ONE whole, never wholes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A non-unit fraction is a stack of unit pieces: 3/4 is three 1/4 pieces.
The top number — the NUMERATOR — counts the pieces taken; the bottom number — the DENOMINATOR — names the cut.
When the top reaches the bottom, the fraction equals 1 — the whole.
Shaded and plain pieces together account for every piece of the bar.
The bottom number cuts, the top number counts — same rule, bigger tops.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every fraction below, say the cut first ("eighths"), then the count ("five of them") — the bottom cuts, the top counts.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Stacks, wholes, and leftovers together.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $5$ equal pieces with $4$ shaded. The shaded fraction is:
problems.explanation: Cut into fifths, $4$ taken: $\frac{4}{5} = 4 \times \frac{1}{5}$ ✓. $\frac{5}{4}$ swaps the jobs; $\frac{1}{5}$ counts the plain piece instead.

problems.prompt: $\frac{5}{9}$ is a stack of:
problems.explanation: Bottom cuts into ninths, top counts five: $5 \times \frac{1}{9} = \frac{5}{9}$ ✓. The second option swaps the numbers' jobs.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $10$ pieces with $7$ shaded. The PLAIN fraction is:
problems.explanation: Plain pieces: $10 - 7 = 3$, and $3 + 7 = 10$ ✓. So $\frac{3}{10}$. $\frac{7}{10}$ is the SHADED part, and $\frac{3}{7}$ compares plain with shaded instead of with the whole.

problems.prompt: Which fraction equals one whole?
problems.explanation: All seven sevenths: $7 \times \frac{1}{7} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{7}{8}$ falls one eighth-piece short, and $\frac{1}{7}$ is a single piece.

problems.prompt: A ger's roof has $6$ equal felt panels; $5$ are already tied on. The tied-on fraction is:
problems.explanation: Cut: sixths. Count: $5$ tied on. $\frac{5}{6} = 5 \times \frac{1}{6}$ ✓ — with $1$ panel, $\frac{1}{6}$, still to go, since $5 + 1 = 6$.

steps.title: You've finished "Non-Unit Fractions"
steps.body: The top number counts stacks of unit pieces, and when it reaches the bottom you hold the whole. Next: putting two fractions side by side and deciding which is bigger — by MEANING, not by tricks.

lessons.title: Comparing Fractions
lessons.concreteComparison: Two same-size chocolate bars, both cut into $8$ pieces. You shade $5$ pieces of yours; your friend shades $3$ of hers. Whose shaded part is bigger? The pieces match exactly — so just COUNT them: $5$ beats $3$. Comparing fractions starts with looking at the pieces, never with tricks.
lessons.objective: Compare two fractions with the same denominator by counting pieces, compare two unit fractions by piece size, and always check that both fractions talk about the same whole.
concept: **Same bottom: count the pieces.** $\frac{5}{8}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$ are stacks of the SAME piece — eighths. Same-size pieces compare by counting: $5 > 3$, so $\frac{5}{8} > \frac{3}{8}$.
**Unit fractions: the bigger bottom loses.** $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{8}$ are ONE piece each, but a $3$-cut makes big pieces and an $8$-cut makes small ones: $\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{8}$.
**Only same wholes compare.** Half of a small khuushuur can be less food than a quarter of a giant one. Fraction comparisons are promises about the SAME whole — check that before comparing anything.
lessons.keyIdea: Same cut: more pieces wins. One piece each: the finer cut loses. And both fractions must talk about the same whole, or the comparison means nothing.

facts.title: Same pieces, just count
facts.explanation: Eighths against eighths — the pieces match, so the bigger count wins.

facts.title: One piece each, size decides
facts.explanation: An 8-cut makes smaller pieces than a 3-cut — the bigger bottom loses.

workedExamples.statement: Compare $\frac{5}{8}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$ of the same bar.
workedExamples.note: The bottoms match — the pieces are the same size.
workedExamples.solution: Both are stacks of eighth-pieces. Count them: $5 > 3$, so $\frac{5}{8} > \frac{3}{8}$.

workedExamples.statement: Compare $\frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{9}$ of the same cake.
workedExamples.note: One piece each — compare the cuts.
workedExamples.solution: One piece each, but a $6$-cut makes bigger pieces than a $9$-cut: $\frac{1}{6} > \frac{1}{9}$, even though $9 > 6$.

commonMistakes.text: Choosing 1/8 over 1/4 because 8 is the bigger number.
commonMistakes.correction: For unit fractions the bottom counts SHARERS: more sharers, smaller shares. 1/8 < 1/4 — the bigger bottom loses.

commonMistakes.text: Comparing fractions of different wholes — half of a small khuushuur against a quarter of a giant one.
commonMistakes.correction: Fractions only compare when they cut the SAME whole. Before writing < or >, check that both fractions talk about one and the same thing.

tryIt.statement: Which is bigger: $\frac{4}{7}$ or $\frac{6}{7}$ of the same bread?
tryIt.solution: Same cut — sevenths — so count the pieces: $6 > 4$, and $\frac{6}{7} > \frac{4}{7}$.

tryIt.statement: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{3}$ or $\frac{1}{8}$ of the same bread?
tryIt.solution: One piece each: the $3$-cut makes bigger pieces than the $8$-cut, so $\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{8}$.

steps.title: Same cut: count the pieces
beats: Two same-size bars, both cut into $8$. The bar below shows $5$ shaded pieces; picture a second bar with only $3$ shaded.
The pieces are IDENTICAL — eighths against eighths — so the comparison is pure counting: $5 > 3$, and $\frac{5}{8} > \frac{3}{8}$.
Whenever the bottoms match, the cut is the same, and the top numbers settle it. The bottom cuts, the top counts — and here only the counting differs.

steps.title: Matching bottoms
steps.intro: Same pieces — the bigger count wins.

examples.prompt: Compare $\frac{5}{8}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$ of the same bar.
steps: Bottoms match: both are stacks of eighth-pieces.

examples.prompt: Order $\frac{2}{6}$, $\frac{5}{6}$, $\frac{3}{6}$ from smallest to biggest.
steps: All sixths — pure counting: $2 < 3 < 5$.

steps.title: Count the matching pieces
steps.intro: Bottoms match, tops decide.

problems.prompt: Which is bigger: $\frac{7}{10}$ or $\frac{9}{10}$ of the same bar?
problems.explanation: Tenths against tenths — count them: $9 > 7$, so $\frac{9}{10} > \frac{7}{10}$.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $\frac{2}{5}$ shaded. Compared with $\frac{4}{5}$ of the same bar, it is:
options: less — $2$ pieces against $4$ of the same size
problems.explanation: Fifths against fifths: $2 < 4$, so $\frac{2}{5} < \frac{4}{5}$. The pieces match, so only the count matters.

problems.prompt: The largest of $\frac{3}{7}$, $\frac{6}{7}$, $\frac{5}{7}$ is:
problems.explanation: All sevenths — count: $6 > 5 > 3$, so $\frac{6}{7}$ wins.

steps.title: Same pieces, just count
steps.prompt: $\frac{5}{9}$ and $\frac{7}{9}$ of the same cake — which is more?
options: $\frac{7}{9}$ — seven pieces beat five of the same size
$\frac{5}{9}$ — the smaller top number means bigger pieces
steps.explanation: Both are stacks of ninth-pieces, so the count decides: $7 > 5$ and $\frac{7}{9} > \frac{5}{9}$. "Smaller number, bigger pieces" is the BOTTOM number's backwards rule, and here the bottoms already match — the pieces are the same size, so only the top count is left to decide. A matching bottom means matching PIECES, not matching amounts.

steps.title: Games are cut into fractions
steps.body: A basketball game is played in four quarters — four equal parts of the playing time, exactly like a bar cut into $4$. Football uses halves instead: two equal parts with the break in the middle. Sports announcers say fraction names all day long.

steps.title: One piece each: the finer cut loses
beats: Now the tops match instead: $\frac{1}{3}$ against $\frac{1}{8}$ — one piece each. The bar below shows the $3$-cut: big, generous pieces.
The $8$-cut shares the SAME whole among far more pieces, so each one is small. One big piece beats one small piece: $\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{8}$.
One warning before any comparing: both fractions must cut the SAME whole. Half of a small khuushuur can be less food than a quarter of a giant one — fractions of different wholes do not compare.

steps.title: Unit against unit
steps.intro: One piece each — the coarser cut wins.

examples.prompt: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{3}$ or $\frac{1}{8}$ of the same bread?
steps: One piece each; the $8$-cut makes small pieces (see the bar).
$\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{8}$ — the bigger bottom loses.

examples.prompt: Order $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{5}$, $\frac{1}{10}$ from biggest to smallest.
steps: Fewest sharers first: $2$-cut, then $5$-cut, then $10$-cut.

steps.title: One piece each
steps.intro: Picture the cut before choosing.

problems.prompt: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{7}$ or $\frac{1}{4}$ of the same cake?
problems.explanation: A $4$-cut makes bigger pieces than a $7$-cut: $\frac{1}{4} > \frac{1}{7}$. Picking $\frac{1}{7}$ because $7 > 4$ reads the bottom forwards — the trap.

problems.prompt: The smallest of $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{9}$ is:
problems.explanation: The finest cut loses: nine pieces share the whole, so $\frac{1}{9} < \frac{1}{6} < \frac{1}{2}$.

problems.prompt: Naran gets $\frac{1}{5}$ of a cake and Bold gets $\frac{1}{8}$ of the SAME cake. Who gets more?
problems.explanation: Same whole, one piece each: the $5$-cut gives bigger pieces than the $8$-cut, so $\frac{1}{5} > \frac{1}{8}$ — Naran. Bold's $8$ only looks bigger.

steps.title: The forwards-reading trap
options: they are equal — both are one piece
steps.explanation: One piece each, so size decides: a $6$-cut shares the whole among fewer pieces than a $9$-cut, so $\frac{1}{6} > \frac{1}{9}$. "$9$ beats $6$" is the forwards-reading trap — unit fractions read backwards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Same bottom: the pieces match, so the bigger count wins.
Unit fractions: one piece each, and the bigger bottom loses.
Never pick a unit fraction just because its bottom number is bigger.
Fractions only compare when they cut the SAME whole.
Every comparison here is done by meaning — picture the pieces.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before each answer, say which case you are in: matching bottoms (count the pieces) or one piece each (the finer cut loses).

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Both comparing rules, side by side.

problems.prompt: The bar shows $\frac{4}{6}$ shaded. Compared with $\frac{1}{6}$ of the same bar:
options: $\frac{4}{6}$ is bigger — four sixths against one
problems.explanation: Matching bottoms: sixths against sixths, and $4 > 1$, so $\frac{4}{6} > \frac{1}{6}$.

problems.prompt: The bar shows one half. Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{2}$ or $\frac{1}{6}$ of the same bar?
problems.explanation: One piece each: a $2$-cut makes far bigger pieces than a $6$-cut, so $\frac{1}{2} > \frac{1}{6}$ — even though $6 > 2$.

problems.prompt: Sara read $\frac{7}{10}$ of a book and Dulguun read $\frac{9}{10}$ of the SAME book. Who read more?
problems.explanation: Same book, same tenth-pieces: $9 > 7$, so $\frac{9}{10} > \frac{7}{10}$ — Dulguun.

problems.prompt: One melon is shared equally by $3$ children, an identical melon by $10$. A bigger piece comes from:
problems.explanation: Fewer sharers, bigger pieces: $\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{10}$. Ten sharers make thin slices of the same melon.

problems.prompt: Which comparison is TRUE?
problems.explanation: Ninths against ninths: $2 < 7$ ✓. The second option falls for the forwards trap ($\frac{1}{5}$ is the BIGGER piece), and the third counts backwards ($3 < 7$ with matching eighths).

steps.title: You've finished "Comparing Fractions"
steps.body: Matching bottoms count pieces; matching tops of $1$ compare cuts — and everything happens on the same whole. Next: fractions leave the chocolate bar and start counting SHEEP — a fraction of a whole set of things.

lessons.title: A Fraction of a Set
lessons.concreteComparison: A herder's $12$ sheep drift into $3$ equal flocks of $4$. One flock — $4$ sheep — is $\frac{1}{3}$ of the herd. Two flocks — $8$ sheep — are $\frac{2}{3}$ of it. The whole is not a bar of chocolate any more: it is a SET of things, and the fraction shares it into groups.
lessons.objective: Find a unit fraction of a set by sharing into equal groups, then a non-unit fraction by taking several of those groups — checking every division by multiplying back.
concept: **The whole can be a set.** $\frac{1}{3}$ OF $12$ sheep: share the $12$ into $3$ equal groups — $12 \div 3 = 4$ in each — and take one group. $\frac{1}{3}$ of $12$ is $4$.
**The bottom cuts the set, the top counts the groups.** For $\frac{2}{3}$ of $12$: the bottom cuts the herd into $3$ groups of $4$; the top takes $2$ of them — $2 \times 4 = 8$ sheep.
**Multiply back to check.** The sharing step is a division, and every division signs a receipt: $12 \div 3 = 4$ because $4 \times 3 = 12$. If the receipt fails, the groups were not equal.
lessons.keyIdea: A fraction of a set is found in two moves: the bottom number shares the set into equal groups, the top number takes that many groups.

facts.title: The bottom shares
facts.explanation: Share into 3 equal groups; one group is one third of the set.

facts.title: The top takes groups
facts.explanation: Two of the three groups — the top number counts groups, not single things.

workedExamples.note: Share the herd into 3 equal groups.
workedExamples.solution: Share: $12 \div 3 = 4$ sheep in each group, and the receipt $4 \times 3 = 12$ ✓ rebuilds the herd. One group is $\frac{1}{3}$ of the herd: $4$ sheep.

workedExamples.note: Same groups — now take two of them.
workedExamples.solution: The groups are already made: $3$ groups of $4$. Take $2$ groups: $2 \times 4 = 8$ sheep. So $\frac{2}{3}$ of $12$ is $8$ — and the third group holds the other $4$, since $8 + 4 = 12$ ✓.

commonMistakes.correction: OF means share, not subtract: cut the 12 into 3 equal groups, 12 ÷ 3 = 4, and one group — 4 — is one third.

commonMistakes.text: Finding 2/3 of 12 by dividing by the top: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
commonMistakes.correction: The bottom shares first: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 in each group. Only then does the top count groups: 2 × 4 = 8.

tryIt.solution: Share into $4$ equal groups: $20 \div 4 = 5$, receipt $5 \times 4 = 20$ ✓. One group — $5$ sweets — is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the bag.
The groups hold $5$ each; take $3$ groups: $3 \times 5 = 15$ sweets. So $\frac{3}{4}$ of $20$ is $15$, with $5$ left in the last group since $15 + 5 = 20$ ✓.

steps.title: Share the set into groups
beats: $\frac{1}{3}$ OF $12$ sheep — the whole is now a HERD, not a bar. The bottom cuts all the same: share the $12$ into $3$ equal groups, as in the picture.
The sharing is a division: $12 \div 3 = 4$ in each group, and the receipt $4 \times 3 = 12$ ✓ rebuilds the herd.
Take ONE group: $4$ sheep. That is $\frac{1}{3}$ of $12$. The bottom number cuts — even when the whole is a flock of animals.

steps.title: Unit fraction of a set
steps.intro: Share into bottom-many groups; take one.

examples.prompt: Find $\frac{1}{4}$ of $20$ sweets.
steps: Share into $4$ equal groups: $20 \div 4 = 5$, receipt $5 \times 4 = 20$ ✓.
One group is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the bag: $5$ sweets.

examples.prompt: Find $\frac{1}{5}$ of $30$ goats.
steps: Share into $5$ equal groups: $30 \div 5 = 6$, receipt $6 \times 5 = 30$ ✓.
One group — $6$ goats — is $\frac{1}{5}$ of the herd.

steps.title: One group of the set
steps.intro: Share first, then take one group.

problems.prompt: $\frac{1}{2}$ of $18$ khuushuur is:
problems.explanation: Share into $2$ equal groups: $18 \div 2 = 9$, receipt $9 \times 2 = 18$ ✓. $16$ subtracts the $2$ instead of sharing — the OF-means-share rule.

problems.prompt: $\frac{1}{3}$ of $15$ horses is:
problems.explanation: Share into $3$ equal groups: $15 \div 3 = 5$, receipt $5 \times 3 = 15$ ✓. $12$ is $15 - 3$ — subtraction wearing a fraction costume.

problems.prompt: $24$ buuz are shared onto $6$ plates, as in the picture. $\frac{1}{6}$ of the buuz is:
problems.explanation: Share into $6$ equal groups: $24 \div 6 = 4$, receipt $4 \times 6 = 24$ ✓. One plate — $4$ buuz — is $\frac{1}{6}$ of the batch.

steps.title: What OF does
options: share $16$ into $4$ equal groups and take one — $4$
steps.explanation: OF shares: $16 \div 4 = 4$ in each group, receipt $4 \times 4 = 16$ ✓, and one group is the answer. Taking $4$ away gives $12$ — subtraction, a different question entirely.

steps.title: One third of every day
steps.body: A day holds $24$ hours, and $24 \div 3 = 8$ — so $8$ hours of sleep is exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of a whole day. Many people sleep about that much, which means about one third of a whole life is spent asleep.

steps.title: Take more than one group
beats: $\frac{2}{3}$ of $12$: the bottom has already done its work — $3$ groups of $4$. Now the TOP counts groups: take $2$ of them, the green groups in the picture.
Two groups of $4$: $2 \times 4 = 8$ sheep. So $\frac{2}{3}$ of $12$ is $8$ — and the grey group keeps the other $4$, since $8 + 4 = 12$ ✓.
The rule in full: the bottom number cuts the set into equal groups, the top number counts the groups you take. Same rule as the chocolate bar — the pieces are just groups now.

steps.title: Non-unit fraction of a set
steps.intro: Bottom shares, top takes groups.

examples.prompt: Find $\frac{2}{3}$ of $12$ sheep.
steps: Share: $12 \div 3 = 4$ in each group, receipt $4 \times 3 = 12$ ✓.
Take $2$ groups: $2 \times 4 = 8$ sheep.

examples.prompt: Find $\frac{3}{4}$ of $20$ sweets.
steps: Share: $20 \div 4 = 5$ in each group, receipt $5 \times 4 = 20$ ✓.
Take $3$ groups: $3 \times 5 = 15$ sweets — the grey group keeps the last $5$.

steps.title: Groups taken, groups left
steps.intro: Share, take, and account for the rest.

problems.prompt: $\frac{2}{5}$ of $15$ sweets is:
problems.explanation: Share: $15 \div 5 = 3$ each, receipt $3 \times 5 = 15$ ✓. Take $2$ groups: $2 \times 3 = 6$. Answering $3$ stops after the sharing step.

problems.prompt: $\frac{3}{8}$ of $24$ buuz is:
problems.explanation: Share: $24 \div 8 = 3$ each, receipt $3 \times 8 = 24$ ✓. Take $3$ groups: $3 \times 3 = 9$. Answering $3$ stops after the sharing step, and $8$ divides by the TOP number ($24 \div 3 = 8$) instead of by the bottom one.

problems.prompt: $\frac{3}{3}$ of $12$ horses is:
options: $12$ — all three groups, the whole herd
problems.explanation: Share: $12 \div 3 = 4$ each. Take ALL $3$ groups: $3 \times 4 = 12$ — the whole herd, because a fraction whose top meets its bottom equals $1$.

steps.title: Top counts groups
steps.explanation: Share: $18 \div 3 = 6$ in each group, receipt $6 \times 3 = 18$ ✓. Take $2$ groups: $2 \times 6 = 12$. Answering $6$ takes only one group; $9$ is half the herd, a different fraction.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The whole can be a SET — a herd, a bag, a batch of buuz.
The bottom number shares the set into equal groups (a division, with its receipt).
A unit fraction of a set is one group.
The top number counts how many groups you take: 2/3 of 12 is 2 groups of 4.
The bottom cuts, the top counts — bars, breads, and herds alike.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Two moves every time: share by the bottom (and sign the division receipt), then take top-many groups. Say both moves before you compute.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Fractions of sets, unit and non-unit.

problems.prompt: $10$ aaruul pieces are shared into $5$ equal groups, as shown. $\frac{1}{5}$ of them is:
problems.explanation: Share: $10 \div 5 = 2$ each, receipt $2 \times 5 = 10$ ✓. One group is $2$ pieces. $8$ subtracts instead of sharing.

problems.prompt: $\frac{3}{5}$ of $20$ togrog coins is:
problems.explanation: Share: $20 \div 5 = 4$ each, receipt $4 \times 5 = 20$ ✓. Take $3$ groups: $3 \times 4 = 12$ coins. $4$ stops after sharing; $15$ took $3$ quarters instead of $3$ fifths.

problems.prompt: $\frac{1}{2}$ of $16$ khuushuur is:
problems.explanation: Share into $2$ groups: $16 \div 2 = 8$, receipt $8 \times 2 = 16$ ✓. $14$ subtracts the $2$ — OF shares, never subtracts.

problems.prompt: $\frac{2}{5}$ of a herd of $25$ goats are white. The white goats number:
problems.explanation: Share: $25 \div 5 = 5$ each, receipt $5 \times 5 = 25$ ✓. Take $2$ groups: $2 \times 5 = 10$ white goats. $5$ stops after one group, and $15$ counts the OTHER three groups — the goats that are not white, since $10 + 15 = 25$ ✓.

problems.prompt: $\frac{5}{6}$ of $30$ sweets is:
problems.explanation: Share: $30 \div 6 = 5$ each, receipt $5 \times 6 = 30$ ✓. Take $5$ groups: $5 \times 5 = 25$. Answering $5$ stops at one group.

steps.title: You've finished "A Fraction of a Set" — and the topic
steps.body: Equal parts, unit pieces, stacks of them, honest comparisons, and fractions that count sheep: the whole meaning of a fraction, drawn one bar and one herd at a time. The bottom number cuts, the top number counts — carry that sentence into Grade 5, where fractions learn many names and start to add.

practice.statement: The bar shows $4$ equal parts with $1$ shaded. Name the shaded part in words and as a fraction.
practice.solution: Four equal parts are quarters; one of them is one quarter, $\frac{1}{4}$. Four such parts rebuild the bar: $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ✓.
One piece each, so the coarsest cut wins: $\frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{5} > \frac{1}{8}$ — the bigger bottom loses.

practice.statement: The bar shows $6$ equal pieces with $5$ shaded. Write the shaded fraction and the plain fraction.
practice.solution: Shaded: $5$ pieces of the sixth size, $\frac{5}{6}$. Plain: the remaining $1$ piece, $\frac{1}{6}$, since $1 + 5 = 6$ accounts for every piece and together they make the whole bar.

practice.statement: Which is more: $\frac{4}{9}$ or $\frac{7}{9}$ of the same cake?
practice.solution: Matching bottoms mean matching pieces — ninths — so count: $7 > 4$, and $\frac{7}{9} > \frac{4}{9}$.

practice.statement: Which is more: $\frac{1}{6}$ or $\frac{1}{10}$ of the same melon?
practice.solution: One piece each: a $6$-cut makes bigger pieces than a $10$-cut, so $\frac{1}{6} > \frac{1}{10}$ — even though $10 > 6$.

practice.statement: $24$ sweets are shared into $4$ equal groups, as shown. Find $\frac{1}{4}$ of the sweets.
practice.solution: Share: $24 \div 4 = 6$ in each group, receipt $6 \times 4 = 24$ ✓. One group — $6$ sweets — is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the bag.
The groups hold $6$ each; take $3$ groups: $3 \times 6 = 18$ sweets. So $\frac{3}{4}$ of $24$ is $18$, and the last group keeps $6$, since $18 + 6 = 24$ ✓.

practice.statement: One of the fractions $\frac{9}{9}$ and $\frac{9}{10}$ equals one whole. Which one, and why?
practice.solution: $\frac{9}{9}$: the top has reached the bottom, so all nine ninth-pieces are taken — $9 \times \frac{1}{9} = 1$ ✓. $\frac{9}{10}$ stops one tenth-piece short of the whole.

testYourself.statement: A pizza is cut into $8$ equal slices and you take $3$, as shown. What fraction did you take, and what fraction remains?
testYourself.solution: Taken: $3$ slices of the eighth size, $\frac{3}{8}$. Remaining: $8 - 3 = 5$ slices, $\frac{5}{8}$, and $5 + 3 = 8$ ✓ accounts for the whole pizza.

testYourself.statement: A cake is cut into $4$ parts of different sizes. Is one of those parts a quarter of the cake? Explain.
testYourself.solution: No. A quarter is one of $4$ EQUAL parts — four true quarters rebuild the cake, $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ✓. Unequal parts carry no fraction name, however many there are.
One piece each — the coarsest cut wins: $\frac{1}{2} > \frac{1}{4} > \frac{1}{7}$. The bigger bottom always loses among unit fractions.

testYourself.statement: Which is bigger: $\frac{5}{12}$ or $\frac{11}{12}$ of the same bar? Say why in one sentence.
testYourself.solution: Matching bottoms, so the pieces match — twelfths — and counting decides: $11 > 5$, so $\frac{11}{12} > \frac{5}{12}$.

testYourself.statement: Find $\frac{2}{5}$ of $20$ khuushuur, showing both moves.
testYourself.solution: Share: $20 \div 5 = 4$ in each group, receipt $4 \times 5 = 20$ ✓. Take $2$ groups: $2 \times 4 = 8$ khuushuur. So $\frac{2}{5}$ of $20$ is $8$.

testYourself.statement: Bataa says $\frac{1}{8} > \frac{1}{4}$ because $8 > 4$. Explain his mistake and write the true comparison.
testYourself.solution: The bottom counts how many pieces SHARE the whole: eight sharers get smaller pieces than four. So $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{4}$ — for unit fractions the bigger bottom loses, and reading $8 > 4$ forwards is exactly the trap.
